digest.top_line: Gomez LCT randomized phase II: mOS 41.2 vs 17.0 mo (P=.017), mPFS 14.2 vs 4.4 mo with RT/surgery to all sites in ≤3-met NSCLC after front-line therapy.
digest.tldr: LCT to all sites in oligometastatic NSCLC more than doubled mOS (41.2 vs 17.0 mo), though accrual stopped at 49 of 94 planned. In high-risk endometrial, PORTEC-3 CRT raised 5y FFS (HR 0.71) but not OS over pelvic RT alone, which held pelvic control at 91%. Brachy dosimetry and an HPV+ OPSCC risk model round it out.

sites.intro: Adjuvant endometrial: PORTEC-3 defines what chemo adds to pelvic RT, plus two dosimetry papers on vaginal cuff brachy.

studies.name: Postoperative endometrial cancer with electronic brachytherapy (Axxent)
studies.tldr: Axxent eBT vs replanned Ir-192 HDR: bladder D2cc 63.8% vs 70.1%, rectum 61.2% vs 68.4% of prescription; one G2 acute toxicity in 94 pts.
details: 🔍 Single-centre series, N=94 postop endometrial pts treated with Axxent 50 kVp eBT, Sept 2015 to Oct 2017
🔍 Same 94 CTs replanned a posteriori for Ir-192 and Co-60 (282 plans); dosimetric comparison, not a clinical comparator arm

subdetails: eBT alone: 25 Gy in 5 fx, n=37 (stage IA plus seven IB1)
Pelvic EBRT 23 × 2 Gy then eBT 15 Gy in 3 fx, n=57
Prescribed at 5 mm from cylinder; PTV = active length + 5 mm
Cylinders 2.5 to 3.5 cm diameter; 33 pts (35%) had prior chemo

details.text: 📊 Mean OAR dose, eBT vs Ir-192 HDR plans

details: 📊 Co-60 plans similar to Ir-192 per authors
📊 V150/V200 higher with eBT; gap narrows as cylinder diameter increases

subdetails: Acute phase: only one G2 event across all pts

details.text: 📊 31 pts with ≥12 mo follow-up (median 19 mo): no recurrence

details: ⚠️ Prescription not RBE-corrected: mean energy 26 vs 355 keV for Ir-192; cited RBE 1.29 to 1.85 at 5 mm
⚠️ OAR reductions are physical dose under TG-43, no heterogeneity correction
⚠️ Mean f/u 14 mo (4 to 25); late vaginal, GI, GU toxicity and cuff recurrence not assessable

verdict.rationale: Single-centre uncontrolled series, 14 mo mean f/u; HDR comparison is replanning, not a treated arm; no late toxicity or local control data at meaningful follow-up.
verdict.audience: Postop endometrial cancer, FIGO IA to IVA, adjuvant VBT ± pelvic EBRT

studies.significance: The prescription copied Ir-192 doses onto a 26 keV source with no RBE adjustment, so the OAR %PD reductions are physical-dose figures and the higher V150/V200 sits at the mucosa. Low acute mucositis at 25 Gy/5 fx and 15 Gy/3 fx is reassuring, but vaginal stenosis and late effects are untested here.
studies.monday_clinic: In postop endometrial pts needing vaginal cuff brachytherapy at a centre with no HDR afterloader, this supports eBT as feasible on acute toxicity; it does not inform late vaginal toxicity or cuff control vs Ir-192 HDR.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-centre series of **94 pts** treated with Axxent eBT, Sept 2015 to Oct 2017. Each eBT plan was **replanned a posteriori** for Ir-192 and Co-60 (282 plans); toxicity scored by RTOG. Mean follow-up **14 mo (4 to 25)**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Postoperative endometrial cancer, mean age 65.9 (33 to 84), FIGO IA through IVA. 33 pts (35%) received chemo before RT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **eBT alone 25 Gy/5 fx** (n=37, stage IA plus seven IB1) or **pelvic EBRT 23 × 2 Gy then eBT 15 Gy/3 fx** (n=57), twice weekly. Dose prescribed at **5 mm** from a 2.5 to 3.5 cm cylinder; 50 kVp source, TG-43 planning, **no RBE correction**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Only **one G2** acute event. At 1 month, vaginal G1 5.3%, rectal G1 1.1%, urinary G1 2.1%, **no G2**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PORTEC-2 established vaginal brachytherapy as adjuvant RT for high-intermediate risk disease using conventional HDR; this series does not test eBT against that clinical benchmark. A cited multicentre eBT series reported bladder V50% 11.5 ± 9.7% and rectum 17.4 ± 10.9%, in the same range as here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents postop endometrial pts receiving cylinder-based vaginal cuff brachytherapy, alone or after pelvic EBRT, at a centre using a 50 kVp eBT unit. Does not represent pts needing interstitial or cervical brachytherapy, or anyone needing late-toxicity or recurrence data.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Higher V150/V200 places hotter dose at the vaginal mucosa, where late stenosis would show and 14 mo cannot capture it. TG-43 without heterogeneity correction may misstate low-energy dose in tissue.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The OAR advantage comes from rapid dose fall-off at low energy, the same property that concentrates dose near the applicator surface. Whether **uncorrected RBE** translates into more late mucosal toxicity, or whether RBE-based de-escalation would cost control, remains open.

studies.interpretation:
The question this series answers is narrower than its conclusion suggests. It shows that a 50 kVp electronic source, run with the same prescription and cylinder geometry as a conventional afterloader, delivers less physical dose to bladder and rectum and produces very little acute toxicity in 94 women. That is useful to know, but it is a planning result plus an uncontrolled toxicity audit, and the comparator never treated anyone. The Ir-192 and Co-60 plans were computed retrospectively on the same CT datasets, so the comparison isolates source physics and nothing else. That makes the dosimetric difference clean and the clinical difference unmeasured.

The central issue a radiation oncologist should weigh is radiobiology. The authors prescribed eBT without correcting for relative biological effectiveness, despite a mean beam energy of 26 keV against 355 keV for Ir-192, and they cite RBE estimates of 1.29 to 1.85 relative to Ir-192 at 5 mm. Read one way, that means the bladder and rectal reductions they report in percent of prescription are understated as biological sparing for those organs at depth, and work by Rava et al. cited in the paper points in that direction for BED3. Read the other way, the vaginal mucosa sits closest to the source, where V150 and V200 were already higher with eBT, and the same RBE logic implies a biologically hotter surface dose. Acute mucositis was low, but mucosal late effects such as stenosis and telangiectasia are the toxicities that would express that excess, and they cannot appear within a mean 14 months.

The absence of recurrence carries limited weight. Only 31 pts had reached 12 months, and vaginal cuff recurrence after adjuvant brachytherapy is uncommon enough that a series this size and duration could not distinguish eBT from HDR even if a real deficit existed. The authors themselves note that dose de-escalation for RBE could compromise control, citing a skin series where reduced dosing lowered tumour control, which frames the trade-off honestly: the prescription choice here leans toward control at a possible mucosal cost.

Against the context of PORTEC-2, which established vaginal brachytherapy as adjuvant therapy for high-intermediate risk disease with conventional sources, eBT is being offered as a substitute delivery device rather than a new treatment. The case for it is logistical: no shielded vault, no isotope exchange, portability. For a department without an afterloader, the acute safety data make eBT a defensible choice. For a department with one, this paper gives no clinical reason to switch, and the calculation method (TG-43, no heterogeneity correction) adds uncertainty to the low-energy dose estimates themselves. What would change the read is multi-year follow-up with formal late vaginal toxicity scoring and cuff recurrence rates, ideally against a contemporaneous HDR cohort.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Ir-192 prescriptions were applied to a 26 keV source without RBE correction (cited RBE 1.29 to 1.85 at 5 mm), so the bladder and rectal %PD reductions are physical dose and the mucosa carries higher V150/V200. Acute toxicity at 25 Gy/5 fx and 15 Gy/3 fx was low; late vaginal effects remain untested.

open_questions: Late vaginal mucosal toxicity with uncorrected RBE
Vaginal cuff control vs Ir-192 HDR at longer follow-up

studies.name: PORTEC-3
studies.tldr: 5y FFS 75.5% vs 68.6% (HR 0.71, p=0.022) with CRT over pelvic RT alone; co-primary 5y OS 81.8% vs 76.7% not met (HR 0.76, p=0.11).
details: 🔍 Open-label randomised phase 3, 103 centres, GCIG; N=660 analysed (330 vs 330), median f/u 60.2 mo
🔍 High-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009 stage I-III: EEC grade 3 with deep MI and/or LVSI, EEC stage II-III, or serous/clear cell
💊 RT alone: 48.6 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions, 5 days/wk
💊 CRT: cisplatin 50 mg/m² x2 during RT, then 4 cycles carboplatin AUC5 + paclitaxel 175 mg/m²
🔍 Vaginal brachy boost in 47% (46% CRT vs 48% RT), mainly for cervical involvement; balanced by arm

details.text: 📊 Co-primary endpoints, stage subgroups, toxicity (CRT vs RT alone)

details: 📊 Pelvic control 91% with RT alone; chemo not needed for locoregional control
📊 Stage III: 11% absolute FFS gain, exceeding the 10% design target
⚠️ OS underpowered: 136 events, 69% of required; time-based final analysis
⚠️ Chemo completion: all 4 cycles carboplatin 79%, paclitaxel 71%; discontinued in 18%
🔗 vs NSGO-EC-9501/EORTC-55991 + ManGO Iliade pooled (n=534): PFS 78% vs 69%, OS trend 82% vs 75%
🔗 vs GOG-258 (abstract): chemo alone vs CRT, no OS/RFS difference but more vaginal and pelvic/para-aortic recurrence without RT

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase 3 met co-primary FFS but missed OS with only 69% of required OS events; direction matches pooled NSGO-EC-9501/ManGO data. Toxicity cost tempers adoption.
verdict.audience: High-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009 stage I-III, post-hysterectomy

studies.significance: Pelvic control was 91% with RT alone, so chemotherapy is not buying locoregional control here; 48.6 Gy pelvic EBRT (plus brachy boost in 47%, balanced by arm) stays the backbone in both arms. The RT question left open is whether pelvic RT can be dropped once chemo is given, which GOG-258 tests and its abstract suggests costs vaginal and nodal control.
studies.monday_clinic: In stage III high-risk endometrial cancer, this supports discussing concurrent cisplatin plus adjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel with pelvic RT for failure-free survival; in stage I-II disease the FFS estimate (HR 0.85, p=0.47) does not clearly justify the added toxicity.

primary_endpoint.name: Overall survival (co-primary with failure-free survival)
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: 95% CI 0.54–1.06, p=0.11, OS not met; co-primary FFS HR 0.71, p=0.022

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Open-label, international, **randomised phase 3** at 103 centres across six GCIG groups; 1:1 by biased-coin minimisation, stratified by centre, lymphadenectomy, stage and histology. 686 enrolled, **660 in the ITT analysis**; median follow-up **60.2 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **High-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009**: stage IA EEC grade 3 with LVSI, IB EEC grade 3, EEC stage II or III, or **serous / clear cell stage IA (with invasion) to III**. WHO PS 0-2, no upper age limit; median age 62, stage III in 46% vs 43%.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Experimental arm added **cisplatin 50 mg/m² x2 concurrent**, then **4 cycles carboplatin AUC5 + paclitaxel 175 mg/m²**. Both cisplatin cycles completed by 92%; all 4 carboplatin and paclitaxel cycles by 79% and 71%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Pelvic EBRT **48.6 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions** in both arms; 45.0-50.4 Gy delivered in 100% vs 98%. **Vaginal brachy boost** for cervical invasion, given in 46% vs 48%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary: overall survival and failure-free survival**, ITT, Cox-adjusted for stratification factors.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **G3+ AEs during treatment 60% vs 12%** (p<0.0001). **G2+ neuropathy persisted at 3y in 8% vs 1%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Direction matches the pooled **NSGO-EC-9501/EORTC-55991 + ManGO Iliade** analysis (PFS 78% vs 69%, OS trend 82% vs 75%), here in a larger trial with concurrent plus adjuvant chemo. **GOG-249** found chemo + VBT no better than pelvic EBRT in stage I-II with more pelvic and para-aortic recurrence; the **GOG-258** abstract reported no OS/RFS gain for CRT over chemo alone but more vaginal and nodal failures without RT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents high-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009 stage I-III after hysterectomy, fit for platinum doublet, with stage III carrying the FFS gain. Does not represent stage IV disease or settings comparing CRT against chemotherapy alone.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Final analysis was **time-based**, with OS events at **69% of the number required**, so a 5% OS difference was below what the trial could detect. RT plan QA outside ANZGOG was still pending, and the stage and age subgroup reads are exploratory.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: CRT buys **FFS, not OS, at 5y**, at the price of a fivefold G3+ toxicity rate and persistent neuropathy. The authors read the stage I-II FFS gain as **not outweighing toxicity**, so the combined regimen fits individual counselling, mainly in stage III.

studies.interpretation:
The trial asked what systemic therapy adds on top of a fixed pelvic RT backbone, and the answer at five years is a failure-free survival gain without a confirmed survival gain. That framing matters for an RT reader. Pelvic RT was given in both arms, pelvic control was already 91% with radiotherapy alone, and the brachytherapy boost was balanced between groups, so nothing in this trial suggests chemotherapy improves locoregional control. Whatever chemotherapy contributes, it contributes beyond the pelvis, and the high proportion of deaths from endometrial cancer in both arms points to systemic failure as the unresolved problem.

The OS result should be read as underpowered rather than as a clean negative. Event rates ran lower than planned, the final analysis was triggered by time rather than events, and only 69% of the required OS events had accrued. A hazard ratio of 0.76 with an upper bound of 1.06 is compatible with a real but modest survival benefit and also with none. The unadjusted and adjusted estimates differ (FFS HR 0.76 unadjusted, p=0.067, versus 0.71 adjusted, p=0.022), which is a reminder that the co-primary that did clear its bar did so narrowly and depended on the prespecified Cox adjustment. The authors themselves call for continued follow-up, and that is the honest read.

Against prior randomised data the result is consistent rather than surprising. The pooled NSGO-EC-9501/EORTC-55991 and ManGO Iliade analysis showed the same pattern, a progression-free gain and a survival trend, with sequential chemotherapy in a cohort carrying fewer stage III patients. PORTEC-3 reproduces that signal at larger scale with a concurrent-then-adjuvant schedule derived from RTOG 9708. What it does not do is settle the question GOG-258 asks: whether radiotherapy remains necessary once a platinum doublet is given. The GOG-249 experience in stage I-II, where replacing pelvic EBRT with chemotherapy plus vaginal brachytherapy increased pelvic and para-aortic recurrence, and the GOG-258 abstract reporting more vaginal and nodal failures with chemotherapy alone, both argue that the pelvic field is doing real work and that omission would trade locoregional control for convenience.

The stage split is where the decision sits. Stage III pts had the largest absolute FFS gain, which the authors note exceeded the 10% difference the trial was designed around, while the stage I-II FFS estimate had a confidence interval spanning one. Read with a G3+ toxicity rate of 60% versus 12% and neuropathy persisting at three years in 8%, the stage I-II benefit is hard to defend for routine use. The older-age and serous-histology signals are interesting, particularly given the authors' caution about selection of fitter older women, but they come from exploratory subgroups and should not drive treatment on their own.

For the trial to be wrong in its practical message, the FFS gain would have to be an artefact of the stratification adjustment or of imbalance in a subgroup, and the consistent direction across prior pooled data makes that less likely. The more plausible risk is overgeneralisation: applying a stage III-weighted benefit to every high-risk pt, including stage I-II disease where the toxicity cost clearly dominates.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pelvic control was 91% with RT alone, so chemo adds nothing locoregionally and 48.6 Gy pelvic EBRT plus indicated brachy boost stays the backbone. The RT decision this trial leaves open is omission of pelvic RT once chemo is given, where GOG-249 and the GOG-258 abstract both show more pelvic and nodal failure without it.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The regimen is demanding: all 4 carboplatin and paclitaxel cycles were completed by 79% and 71%, G3+ AEs ran 60% vs 12%, and G2+ neuropathy persisted at 3y in 8%. The FFS gain concentrates in stage III, and the authors flag a larger benefit in women over 70 and at least as much benefit in serous or clear cell histology.

open_questions: Does the OS difference emerge with longer follow-up?
Is pelvic RT still needed in stage III when chemotherapy is given?
Can stage I-II pts be spared chemotherapy toxicity safely?

studies.name: HDR vaginal brachytherapy cylinder dosimetry
studies.tldr: Surface SD 6% vs 18% with surface vs 0.5-cm depth prescription (2-cm cylinder). Omitting dome optimization points gave hot spots >150% and cold spots <60%.

details.text: 🔍 Treatment-planning physics study (Henry Ford, Plato BPS 14.2.4); no patients, no clinical endpoints
🔍 Single-channel CT/MR and radiographic cylinders, 2.0-4.0 cm diameter, active length 3-8 cm
🔍 Compared surface (P0) vs 0.5-cm depth (P5) prescription, each with and without curved-end optimization points (NEP)

details: 📊 Surface SD 6% (P0) vs 18% (P5), 2-cm cylinder, 0.8-cm tip space
📊 Without dome points: extreme hot (>150%) and cold (<60%) spots

details.text: 📊 NEP failure modes by tip space (2-cm cylinder)
subdetails: 0.8-cm tip: MD at depth down ~10%, apex cold spots 50-65%
0.5-cm tip, surface Rx: MD up ~10%, apex surface hot spots 140-170%
0.5-cm tip, P5NEP: target MD on depth, but surface SD 25%

details: 📊 Shorter tip space raises dosimetric uncertainty >30%
📐 Surface-dose magnification M ≈ 1.00 + 0.64/L + 1.23/S (cm); matched plans within 2%

details.text: 📐 Worked example: 7 Gy at 0.5 cm, 3-cm cylinder, 5-cm length → 10.8 Gy to surface (M = 1.54)
🔗 Context: ABS survey cited, >90% of users prescribe to 0.5 cm; >one tenth omit dome points

details: ⚠️ The conclusion that surface Rx is optimal is a dosimetric argument; no toxicity or vaginal-control data were collected

details.text: ⚠️ Single vendor TPS and applicators, 2007-era point-based optimization; transfer to modern 3D planning not tested

details: ⚠️ The regression for M comes from 2 lengths × 2 diameters; extrapolation beyond that grid is unvalidated

verdict.rationale: Planning-system dosimetry with no patients or outcomes. 'Surface prescription is optimal' rests on mucosal dose uniformity, a surrogate never tied to toxicity or vaginal control here.
verdict.audience: Post-hysterectomy endometrial cancer, adjuvant HDR vaginal cuff brachytherapy

studies.significance: The actionable physics: the dome needs optimization points. Without them the apex runs cold (50-65%) or hot (140-170%) depending on tip space, and the 0.5-cm depth prescription hides surface SD up to 18%. If you switch to a surface prescription, M = 1.00 + 0.64/L + 1.23/S gives the surface dose that keeps the 0.5-cm dose unchanged.
studies.monday_clinic: For post-hysterectomy endometrial pts on single-channel cylinder VBT, this supports checking that apex and dome points are in the optimization and reporting both surface and 0.5-cm doses. It gives no outcome evidence for changing an established 0.5-cm depth prescription.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: A **treatment-planning study** with no patients. Plato BPS 14.2.4 plans were built on Nucletron radiographic cylinders (tip space ~0.5 cm) and CT/MR-compatible cylinders (tip space 0.6-0.8 cm). Dose uniformity at each depth was measured as the mean dose (MD) and SD across dose points spaced evenly around the dome and along the cylinder.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Cylinders were **2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5 and 4.0 cm** in diameter, with active lengths of **3 to 8 cm** (upper third to the whole vagina). Prescription was to the **surface (P0)** or to **0.5-cm depth (P5)**, with or without optimization points on the curved end (NEP). The worked illustration used 7 Gy × 3 fractions.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary measures:** MD and SD at the surface and at 0.5-cm depth. Dose fall-off was the ratio of MD at 0.75 cm to MD at 0.5 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Surface prescription gave **surface SD 6% vs 18%** with P5 (2-cm cylinder, 0.8-cm tip), with **almost the same fall-off** beyond 0.5 cm. NEP plans produced **hot spots >150% and cold spots <60%**. A shorter tip space raised dosimetric uncertainty **>30%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The paper frames its result against the ABS 2000 guidance (dome optimization points, report doses at both surface and 0.5 cm) and an ABS survey in which **>90%** prescribe to 0.5 cm. It also cites Sorbe's randomized 2.5 vs 5.0 Gy × 6 trial, in which higher dose increased atrophy, bleeding and shortening.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents single-channel cylinder HDR VBT planned with point-based optimization around the dome. Does not represent multichannel applicators, image-guided volumetric planning, or any clinical toxicity or control endpoint.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The M regression was fit on only **two lengths × two diameters**, using one vendor's applicators and TPS. The claim that a lower surface dose reduces atrophy and shortening is extrapolated from other trials, not measured.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A 0.5-cm depth prescription delivers its intended depth dose only when dome points are included, and the surface dose it gives varies with cylinder size and tip space. Prescribing to the surface with a geometry-scaled dose fixes the surface number. Whether that changes toxicity remains open.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a planning-hygiene argument rather than evidence for a particular prescription convention. Its most defensible finding is the negative one. When the optimizer is given no points on the cylinder dome, the apex dose stops being predictable, and the direction of the error depends on hardware. With the 0.8-cm tip space of the CT/MR-compatible tube, the apex ran cold (50-65%) and the depth mean fell about 10%. With the 0.5-cm tip space of the thin metal tube, the apex surface ran hot (140-170%). The cuff apex is where recurrence risk concentrates, so an omission that silently underdoses it in one applicator and overdoses it in another is a real QA problem. The survey the authors cite says more than one tenth of users were making that omission.

The headline recommendation, prescribing to the surface at a higher dose, is weaker. The authors show that surface prescription flattens mucosal dose (surface SD 6% vs 18% in the 2-cm case) while preserving the 0.5-cm mean and fall-off. They then reason that a lower and more uniform surface dose should reduce atrophy, bleeding and shortening. That last step borrows its clinical footing from Sorbe's randomized dose comparison, which tested dose per fraction rather than prescription point. Nothing in this dataset links surface SD to a toxicity outcome. The recommendation may be right, but here it is a hypothesis built on a surrogate.

The magnification factor M = 1.00 + 0.64/L + 1.23/S is useful arithmetic for anyone converting between conventions, and the paper's own example (7 Gy at 0.5 cm becoming 10.8 Gy at the surface for a 3-cm cylinder and 5-cm length) shows how far the two prescriptions sit apart. It also shows how easily a surface prescription copied from the literature can underdose depth when the cylinder is large. The regression was fit on a small geometric grid with a single planning system. A reader should check it against their own TPS before trusting it outside 3-5 cm lengths.

Two things would have to be true for the practical conclusion to fail. First, modern volumetric or library-based plans might already have closed the dome-point gap. Second, surface inhomogeneity at these magnitudes might not drive late vaginal toxicity once dose per fraction is held constant. Neither question is addressed here. The durable takeaway is procedural: put points on the dome, know your tip space, and report surface and 0.5-cm doses together, whatever point you prescribe to.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The actionable physics: the dome needs optimization points. Without them the apex runs cold (50-65%) or hot (140-170%) depending on tip space, and the 0.5-cm depth prescription hides surface SD up to 18%. M = 1.00 + 0.64/L + 1.23/S converts a depth dose to its surface equivalent if you switch conventions.

open_questions: Does surface prescription reduce vaginal atrophy or shortening clinically?
Does the M factor hold on modern 3D image-guided planning?

⚠️ OS is the only endpoint; NCDB carries no locoregional recurrence or patterns of failure
⚠️ PNI, close margins and smoking not captured in NCDB, so absent from the model
⚠️ Model derived and scored in the same cohort; no external validation described in source
⚠️ Margins still earn points despite no multivariate mortality association in HPV+
⚠️ Source gives traditional high-risk share two ways: 46.1% (1061/2302) and 45.1% (1038/2302)
🔗 ICON-S staging built on definitive CRT; only 2% surgical, so no pathologic features tested
⚠️ Prognostic, not predictive: OS models adjusted for adjuvant RT/CRT, so no test of RT omission

verdict.rationale: Registry retrospective, OS-only, model scored in its own derivation cohort without external validation; cannot show reclassified pts tolerate less adjuvant RT/CRT.
verdict.audience: Surgically resected HPV+ OPSCC, LN yield ≥15, AJCC 7th T1-4 N0-3 M0

studies.significance: The composite down-weights margins and ENE against T4 and ≥5 nodes, so most traditional high-risk pts become low risk (high-risk share 45.1% to 6.6%). That is the adjuvant CRT escalation trigger. NCDB has OS but no locoregional failure, so it cannot say whether reclassified microscopic-ENE or margin-positive pts keep in-field control with less RT or no chemo.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected HPV+ OPSCC with microscopic ENE or a microscopically positive margin but T1-2 disease and fewer than 5 nodes, this questions reading the case as automatically high risk for CRT escalation; it does not extend to T4 or ≥5-node disease, or to HPV-unassociated HNSCC.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective NCDB cohort**, dx 2010-2013, analyzed 2018-2019. Univariate + multivariate Cox for OS; points assigned to features in proportion to effect size, then the composite was selected on C-index, AIC and clinical judgement.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Upfront surgery + adequate neck dissection (LN yield ≥15)**, non-metastatic T1-4 N0-3 M0 (AJCC 7th). HPV+ OPSCC n=2302 vs HPV-unassociated HNSCC n=13 022; OPSCC without HPV testing and surgery + chemo alone excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: 5-y OS** (KM, log-rank) and **discrimination by C-index**. Multivariate models adjusted for age, sex, race, comorbidity, insurance, adjuvant RT and/or CRT, and hospital type.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: In HPV+ OPSCC only **T stage, LVI, number of LN mets and ENE** tracked with mortality; **margins, LN size, level IV-V and bilateral nodes did not**. Composite C-index **0.67** (3 tiers) vs **0.58** traditional.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The traditional tiers being tested come from NCCN, ASCO, **ECOG 3311** and **PATHOS** definitions, the de-escalation trials that use pathology to allocate adjuvant RT vs CRT. **ICON-S** refined clinical staging for HPV+ disease but was built on definitive CRT with only 2% surgical pts, so it could not weigh pathologic features.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents surgically resected, adequately neck-dissected HPV+ OPSCC staged by AJCC 7th edition. Does not represent HPV-unassociated HNSCC, pts with LN yield below 15, or decisions hinging on PNI or close margins, which the model never saw.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Points include **margins despite no multivariate association**, a judgement call that inflates their weight. The source states the traditional high-risk share inconsistently (46.1% and 45.1%), and HPV testing method is not described.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Traditional HNSCC pathologic tiers are **weakly prognostic** in HPV+ OPSCC, and nodal burden plus T4 matter more than ENE or margins. Whether the reclassified majority can safely receive **less adjuvant therapy** is untested here and belongs to the next deintensification trials.

studies.interpretation:
The core finding is less about the new score than about the failure of the old one. Applied to resected HPV+ OPSCC, the pathologic risk tiers inherited from HPV-unassociated disease separate 5-y OS only from 93.2% to 83.7%, with a C-index of 0.58, barely above chance. The same tiers in HPV-unassociated HNSCC span 76.2% to 40.9% (C-index 0.68). That contrast is the useful signal for a radiation oncologist: the features that trigger adjuvant CRT, ENE and positive margins above all, were calibrated on a disease with a very different natural history, and in this registry they carry less mortality information in HPV+ pts than T4 or a high nodal count.

This sits alongside the reasoning behind ECOG 3311 and PATHOS, which both use pathology to allocate adjuvant intensity after transoral surgery, and it extends what ICON-S could not test, since ICON-S was built on pts treated with definitive CRT and had almost no surgical cases. If the composite is right, the trial-eligible high-risk population is far smaller than current definitions imply: 6.6% rather than 45.1% of this cohort.

Several design choices should lower confidence in that conclusion. First, the endpoint is OS. HPV+ OPSCC deaths are infrequent and partly non-cancer, and NCDB carries no locoregional recurrence, no in-field versus out-of-field failure, and no distant metastasis. The adjuvant RT decision is about locoregional control, and a feature can matter for local failure (a positive margin, say) while barely moving OS, because salvage exists or because events are rare. Second, the multivariate models adjust for adjuvant RT and CRT. A feature like ENE may look weak precisely because those pts received chemo; the model describes prognosis under the treatment they actually got, not prognosis if treatment were withdrawn. That makes it a prognostic tool, not evidence that downgraded pts can skip RT or chemo. Third, the points were chosen partly on clinical judgement and on optimizing C-index in the same data used to report it, with no external validation described, so the 0.67 and 0.73 figures are likely optimistic. Margins were assigned points despite showing no multivariate association, which shows the score is part model, part opinion.

Coding also limits transfer. PNI and close margins, both in the traditional intermediate tier, are not in NCDB, and staging is AJCC 7th edition, which nodal-heavy HPV+ disease has since outgrown. The source also reports the traditional high-risk proportion two different ways, a small but real reproducibility flag.

What this does settle is narrower and still worth keeping: in a large surgical cohort, nodal number and advanced T stage, not ENE extent or margin status, were the pathologic features that tracked survival in HPV+ OPSCC. For anyone designing or enrolling in surgical deintensification trials, that argues for stratifying on nodal burden and T4, and for treating microscopic ENE or a microscopically positive margin as weaker evidence for escalation than current algorithms assume. It would be wrong if prospective data with locoregional endpoints showed reclassified pts failing in field once adjuvant intensity is reduced.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The CRT-escalation triggers, ENE and positive margins, carry little OS weight in HPV+ disease here, while T4 and ≥5 nodes dominate. Without locoregional endpoints and with adjuvant RT/CRT adjusted out, it frames but cannot license reduced adjuvant RT or chemo omission.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Pathologic staging after transoral surgery and neck dissection (LN yield ≥15) is the input: nodal count and T stage drive prognosis, while margin status and LN size, level or laterality do not track mortality. That changes which specimen findings carry weight when counseling on adjuvant needs.

open_questions: Does composite low-risk status predict safe omission of adjuvant RT?
External validation with locoregional recurrence endpoints
Does microscopic ENE alone justify adding concurrent chemo?

studies.name: Gomez LCT oligometastatic NSCLC (long-term results)
studies.tldr: mOS 41.2 vs 17.0 mo (P=.017) and mPFS 14.2 vs 4.4 mo favoring LCT over maintenance/observation in oligometastatic NSCLC after front-line therapy.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase II, 3 institutions, 1:1 LCT vs maintenance therapy or observation (MT/O), unmasked
🔍 Stage IV NSCLC, ≤3 metastases, no progression at ≥3 mo after front-line systemic therapy
🔍 LCT = RT, surgery or both to all active sites; concurrent chemoRT allowed to primary and nodes

details.text: 📊 Outcomes by arm (ITT, median f/u 38.8 mo)

details: 📐 Multivariable Cox (arm, met number, EGFR/ALK): LCT OS HR 0.46 (95% CI 0.21-0.99), P=.048
📊 Crossover: 9 of 20 MT/O progressors got LCT to all lesions; their mOS 17 mo (7.8-NR)
⚠️ RT dose/fractionation not reported in source text (Appendix Table A1)
⚠️ DSMB closed accrual at 49 of 94 planned; early stops for benefit tend to overstate effect
⚠️ Significance threshold P<.10; OS was a secondary endpoint
⚠️ Pre-IO era (opened 2012); front-line and maintenance regimens heterogeneous

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase II closed early for PFS benefit at 49 of 94 planned pts; OS is secondary and tested at P<.10. Needs phase III confirmation (e.g. NRG-LU002).
verdict.audience: Stage IV NSCLC, ≤3 mets, no progression after front-line systemic therapy

studies.significance: The OS gap tracks survival after progression, 37.6 vs 9.4 mo: only 15 of 39 progressors (41%) got LCT at progression, and in the MT/O arm 7 were blocked by polymetastatic progression. That argues for consolidating every site while disease is still oligometastatic, not holding RT for progression. Dose and fractionation are not in source text.
studies.monday_clinic: In stage IV NSCLC with ≤3 metastases and no progression after front-line platinum doublet, EGFR TKI or crizotinib, this supports consolidating all sites over maintenance alone; it does not extend to IO-treated pts, >3 metastases, or disease progressing on first-line therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized phase II**, 1:1, 3 institutions (MD Anderson, London Health Sciences Center, University of Colorado); unmasked. **Closed early by DSMB** after 49 of 74 enrolled pts were randomized (94 planned). Median follow-up **38.8 mo** (28.3-61.4).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Stage IV NSCLC, ≤3 metastases** (primary not counted), ECOG ≤2, **no progression after front-line therapy**: ≥4 cycles platinum doublet, or ≥3 mo EGFR TKI or crizotinib. Randomization dynamically balanced on met number, response, CNS mets, N stage and EGFR/ALK status.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: LCT was RT, surgery or both to **all active disease sites**, modality chosen by MDT; concurrent chemoRT allowed for primary and regional nodes. **Dose and fractionation not reported in source text** (Appendix Table A1).

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** PFS from randomization. **Secondary:** OS, toxicity, time to new lesions. Powered (90%) for PFS 4 to 7 mo, HR 0.57; P<.10 deemed significant.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: PFS, OS and survival-after-progression gains in the arm table above. Late LCT at progression correlated with OS in a multivariable model, HR 0.44 (0.18-1.06), P=.064; initial LCT HR 0.30 (0.12-0.75).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No additional grade ≥3 toxicity** beyond events reported in the initial publication.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors state no prior randomized trial had shown an **OS benefit from LCT in lung cancer**. They align their proposed oligometastatic definition (0-3 metastases, unconstrained by molecular profile) with most pts enrolled on **SABR-COMET** and the **UT Southwestern** randomized phase II trial, and point to **NRG-LU002** as the phase III test.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents stage IV NSCLC with ≤3 metastases that did not progress after platinum doublet or first-line EGFR/ALK TKI. Does not represent IO-treated pts, higher metastatic burden, or disease progressing on front-line therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Unmasked with heterogeneous physician-chosen maintenance. Post-progression and late-LCT analyses are exploratory, post-randomization, and exclude 3 MT/O pts who crossed over before progression. **EGFR/ALK cohort n=8**, too small to read.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The OS gain is carried by **survival after progression**, consistent with a window in which all sites are still treatable. Whether the effect survives IO maintenance and a full-size trial is unsettled.

studies.interpretation:
Before this update, the case for local consolidation in oligometastatic NSCLC rested on retrospective series, single-arm prospective work, and PFS signals from small randomized trials; the authors note that no randomized trial had yet shown an OS benefit from LCT in lung cancer. Converting a PFS result into an OS difference, mOS 41.2 vs 17.0 mo, is why this trial became a reference point alongside SABR-COMET and the UT Southwestern study. It also fixed the eligibility template much later work borrowed: three or fewer metastases, no progression after front-line systemic therapy.

The magnitude deserves skepticism proportional to how the trial ended. The DSMB closed accrual at 49 of a planned 94 after an interim look favored LCT, and trials stopped early for benefit tend to overstate effect size because stopping selects for a favorable random excursion. OS was secondary, tested at a P<.10 threshold, and the intervals are wide: the LCT arm's lower bound is 18.9 mo while the MT/O upper bound reaches 39.8 mo. Only 29 deaths inform the comparison. The multivariable OS HR 0.46 (0.21-0.99) holds after adjusting for metastasis count and EGFR/ALK status, but an upper bound that close to 1 reads as a direction more than a size.

The more informative signal is where the OS gap came from. Survival after progression was 37.6 vs 9.4 mo, while the share receiving late LCT did not differ by arm (P=.39). In the MT/O arm, seven progressors could not receive LCT because progression was polymetastatic. The reading the data most plainly support is a window argument: consolidation is feasible while disease is limited, and deferring it to progression lets a fraction of pts lose eligibility. The late-LCT association, HR 0.44 (0.18-1.06), fits that story, but it is a post-randomization comparison with selection built in, since pts fit and limited enough to get late LCT are prognostically favored.

For RT practice the gap is technique. LCT pooled surgery, RT and chemoRT to primary and nodes at MDT discretion, and dose and fractionation are not in the source text. The trial answers whether to treat all sites, not how much dose, or whether ablative stereotactic dosing outperforms conventional fractionation. The control arm was itself heterogeneous, physician-chosen maintenance or observation, unmasked.

What would make it wrong: the effect is an early-stopping artifact, or it does not persist on an immunotherapy backbone, which the trial (opened 2012) never included. Longer control-arm survival on IO maintenance would compress any absolute gain and could change where the consolidation window sits. The EGFR/ALK subset (n=8) cannot support a molecular claim either way. The authors frame their own subset analyses as provocative rather than paradigm-defining and call for phase III confirmation, NRG-LU002 among them. Until then the data support LCT within this trial's eligibility, not extrapolation to higher burden or IO-treated disease.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The OS gap tracks survival after progression, 37.6 vs 9.4 mo, and 7 MT/O progressors lost LCT eligibility to polymetastatic progression. That argues for consolidating every site while still oligometastatic rather than reserving RT for progression; dose and fractionation are not in source text.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Maintenance or observation was the comparator, and adding LCT gave mOS 41.2 vs 17.0 mo on a pre-IO backbone of platinum doublet, EGFR TKI or crizotinib. Whether the gap persists with IO maintenance, absent from this trial, is the open regimen question.

open_questions: Does the OS benefit hold with IO-era maintenance?
Does LCT add OS in EGFR/ALK-driven oligometastatic NSCLC?
Does a phase III trial confirm the OS benefit?

papers.title: Local Consolidative Therapy Vs. Maintenance Therapy or Observation for Patients With Oligometastatic Non–Small-Cell Lung Cancer: Long-Term Results of a Multi-Institutional, Phase II, Randomized Study
papers.abstract: PURPOSE Our previously published findings reported that local consolidative therapy (LCT) with radiotherapy or surgery improved progression-free survival (PFS) and delayed new disease in patients with oligometastatic non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that did not progress after front-line systemic therapy. Herein, we present the longer-term overall survival (OS) results accompanied by additional secondary end points. PATIENTS AND METHODS This multicenter, randomized, phase II trial enrolled patients with stage IV NSCLC, three or fewer metastases, and no progression at 3 or more months after front-line systemic therapy. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to maintenance therapy or observation (MT/O) or to LCT to all active disease sites. The primary end point was PFS; secondary end points were OS, toxicity, and the appearance of new lesions. All analyses were two sided, and P values less than .10 were deemed significant. RESULTS The Data Safety and Monitoring Board recommended early trial closure after 49 patients were randomly assigned because of a significant PFS benefit in the LCT arm. With an updated median follow-up time of 38.8 months (range, 28.3 to 61.4 months), the PFS benefit was durable (median, 14.2 months [95% CI, 7.4 to 23.1 months] with LCT v 4.4 months [95% CI, 2.2 to 8.3 months] with MT/O; P = .022). We also found an OS benefit in the LCT arm (median, 41.2 months [95% CI, 18.9 months to not reached] with LCT v 17.0 months [95% CI, 10.1 to 39.8 months] with MT/O; P = .017). No additional grade 3 or greater toxicities were observed. Survival after progression was longer in the LCT group (37.6 months with LCT v 9.4 months with MT/O; P = .034). Of the 20 patients who experienced progression in the MT/O arm, nine received LCT to all lesions after progression, and the median OS was 17 months (95% CI, 7.8 months to not reached). CONCLUSION In patients with oligometastatic NSCLC that did not progress after front-line systemic therapy, LCT prolonged PFS and OS relative to MT/O.

papers.title: Postoperative endometrial cancer treatments with electronic brachytherapy source
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose This study is a dosimetric and acute toxicity comparison of endometrial cancer patients treated with either Axxent (Xoft, Inc., San José, CA, USA) electronic and interstitial brachytherapy versus interstitial high dose rate brachytherapy (HDRBT). Materials and Methods Between 2015 and 2017, 94 patients with postoperative endometrial cancer were treated in our centre with the Axxent electronic brachytherapy (eBT) system. The V 150 and V 200 are evaluated prospectively for each plan. The mean age of patients was 65.9 years (age range 33–84 years), with different tumour staging. Of the 94 patients, 37 received exclusive adjuvant brachytherapy (25 Gy in five sessions); the remaining patients received external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with a regimen of 23 sessions of 2 Gy each to the entire pelvis, followed by eBT (15 Gy in three sessions). Additionally, the absorbed doses received by the organs at risk (OAR), urinary bladder, rectum and sigmoid colon were compared with HDRBT plans, evaluating D 2cc , V 50% and V 35% . Median follow-up was done for each of the 94 patients to assess the toxicity of the treatment: vaginal mucosa toxicity, rectal and urinary toxicity; and results are presented for acute toxicity, toxicity at 1 month after the end of treatment and follow-up after 12 months for a portion of patients according to the Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) toxicity criteria. Results The doses in OAR for eBT plans were lower than that for HDRBT plans, both Ir-192 and Co-60 plans, whose doses were similar. The dose in bladder with eBT was 63.8% of the prescribed dose for D 2cc versus 70.1% for HDRBT Ir-192, for V 50% was 7.2% versus 12.7% and for V 35% was 15.2% versus 28.2%. In rectum the D 2cc was 61.2% versus 68.4%, for V 50% was 7.9% versus 14.3% and for V 35% was 16.7% versus 32%. Results demonstrated lower doses to OAR in all eBT plans. Acute toxicity in eBT was very low in cases of mucositis, with only one case of toxicity greater than grade 1, rectal toxicity and urinary toxicity; results at 1 month are equally good, toxicity symptoms disappeared and no relapses have occurred to date. Conclusions The results of treatment with the Axxent eBT unit for 94 patients are very good, as no recurrence has been observed and the toxicity of the treatment is very low. The increase in V 150 and V 200 has not produced an increase in vaginal mucosa toxicity, and the doses in the OAR are lower than in the plans implemented for HDRBT with Ir-192 or Co-60. eBT is a good alternative to treat endometrial cancer in centres without conventional HDR availability. To date, there are limited published studies reporting on outcomes from patients treated with eBT.
